note: Module checks (v1 upgrade, 20/11/2026, draft pending SME sign-off) and the final knowledge check for CARSI Professional Moisture Meters. Original CARSI questions written for Australian and New Zealand conditions; no IICRC standard text reproduced.

quizzes.title: CARSI Professional Moisture Meters — Module 1 check

questions.questionText: A loss adjuster questions your "dry" call on a hallway wall. What makes your reading defensible?
questions.explanation: A statement others can check names the instrument and mode, the location, any correction and the baseline. A verbal assurance or a bare photo of the display cannot be repeated or checked.

questions.questionText: Which skills does this course assume you already have from Psychrometry?
questions.explanation: The course assumes you can already calculate dew point, humidity ratio in g/kg and EMC. Slab drilling, relining and laboratory servicing are not prerequisites for it.

questions.questionText: In this course, a section labelled "CARSI method" or "worked example" is what?
questions.explanation: Those labels mark CARSI's own field method and arithmetic, which you can check with the formula beside it. Quotes and linked paraphrase are labelled differently, and no standard text is copied.

questions.questionText: You need a reading on wet plasterboard beside a double GPO. What goes first?
questions.explanation: Pinless mode scans without piercing anything you have not checked, and you move off the GPO and its service lines before confirming with pins. Pins first risks hitting a cable or pipe.

questions.questionText: On a contaminated job, which area do you test first so you do not spread contamination?
questions.explanation: Testing the unaffected control area first stops you carrying contamination into it on your meter and pins. Starting at the worst area means every later reading risks cross-contamination.

questions.questionText: Why tell the owner before using pins on finished surfaces?
questions.explanation: Pins leave small holes, so the owner should agree first and you should test in inconspicuous places where a reading there answers the question. The other reasons are not what the lesson teaches.

questions.questionText: Which free document explains how pin and pinless meters estimate moisture content?
questions.explanation: The USDA Wood Handbook, chapter 13, explains how electrical meters estimate moisture content. The QBCC guide ties readings to rebuilding decisions instead, and AS 1884:2021 is a paid standard.

questions.questionText: A vinyl installer says your slab is not to the standard. Which paid standards might they mean?
questions.explanation: AS 1884:2021 covers resilient floor coverings and ASTM F2170 covers in situ slab RH testing, and both are paid. The other three are free guides or legislation.

questions.questionText: How does CARSI cite a paid standard?
questions.explanation: CARSI names a paid standard by number and edition and tells you to read the current edition yourself. Describing what a standard requires without having read it is the mistake the lesson warns against.

quizzes.title: CARSI Professional Moisture Meters — Module 2 check

questions.questionText: In the moisture content formula, what is the divisor?
questions.explanation: The formula divides the water by the oven-dry mass, so the dry wood is the fixed yardstick. Dividing by the wet mass would understate the moisture content.

questions.questionText: A specimen weighs 150.0 g wet and 120.0 g oven-dry. What is its moisture content?
questions.explanation: Water is 150.0 − 120.0 = 30.0 g, and 30.0 ÷ 120.0 × 100 = 25%. Dividing by the wet mass instead gives the tempting but wrong 20%.

questions.questionText: Why can very wet wood show a moisture content above 100%?
questions.explanation: The water is divided by the dry mass, so a sample holding more water than its own dry mass passes 100%. It is not a calculation error.

questions.questionText: What do uninsulated pins report?
questions.explanation: Uninsulated pins sense the lowest resistance along their length, so they report the wettest layer touched. They do not average the stud.

questions.questionText: How deep do insulated pins go in a 45 mm stud?
questions.explanation: One-fifth to one-quarter of 45 mm is 9 to 11.25 mm, which reflects the average moisture content of the piece. Deeper pins reach the far face instead.

questions.questionText: A surface reading is higher than the deep reading. What does that suggest?
questions.explanation: A higher surface reading suggests the surface has been rewetted, for example by cleaning, while the core is drier. It does not point to a wet core.

questions.questionText: Which layers dominate a pinless meter reading?
questions.explanation: The field of a pinless meter weakens rapidly with depth, so the surface layers dominate the reading. It does not average the whole thickness.

questions.questionText: How do you confirm a pinless wet band?
questions.explanation: A second pinless scan has the same shallow view. Pins at depth, inside the band and just outside it, measure the spots the scan found.

questions.questionText: A pinless meter reads low on a skirting board, but pins show a wet core. Why?
questions.explanation: Surface layers dominate a pinless reading, so a dry outer layer over a wet core can read low. Pinless meters do not ignore wet timber.

questions.questionText: What does a thermal camera measure?
questions.explanation: A thermal camera measures surface temperature only. A cool patch may be wet, but the camera cannot tell you that without a moisture meter.

questions.questionText: A patch measures 21.5 °C in a room with a 17.0 °C dew point. What follows?
options: It sits below the dew point
It sits above the dew point
It matches the room air temperature
It sits at the dew point
questions.explanation: At 21.5 °C the patch is above the 17.0 °C dew point, so condensation is not the explanation. Condensation needs a surface at or below the dew point.

questions.questionText: What confirms a camera suspect?
questions.explanation: Only a moisture meter gives a moisture reading. A second image shows temperature again and cannot tell a leak from a draught.

questions.questionText: Which instrument finds the edges of a wet area quickly?
questions.explanation: A pinless meter scans a wall quickly and shows where a wet area starts and stops. Pins then confirm the readings at depth.

questions.questionText: What depth do you set for insulated pins in a 19 mm floorboard?
questions.explanation: One-fifth to one-quarter of 19 mm is 3.8 to 4.75 mm, so about 4 to 5 mm. Deeper pins would reach the far face of the board.

questions.questionText: A thermal image shows a cold strip on a ceiling. What next?
questions.explanation: A cold strip can be a draught or missing insulation, so it is not proven wet. A meter reading confirms or clears it before any repair call.

quizzes.title: CARSI Professional Moisture Meters — Module 3 check

questions.questionText: Which reading may be reported as a moisture content percentage?
questions.explanation: A percentage needs a meter calibrated for the material, with corrections applied. Plasterboard, concrete and masonry readings are points even when the display looks like a percentage.

questions.questionText: What is the only fair comparison for 64 points on wet plasterboard?
options: Unaffected plasterboard, same meter, same scale
Timber kickboard reading in the kitchen
A published figure for gypsum plasterboard
Wet plasterboard measured at another property
questions.explanation: Points only mean something against the same material, meter and scale in an unaffected area. A different material, meter or building changes what the number represents.

questions.questionText: Your meter shows 28 on its timber scale pressed on concrete. What do you write?
questions.explanation: The timber scale is not calibrated for concrete, so the number is qualitative points that need an unaffected slab baseline. Calling it a percentage claims more than the meter can say.

questions.questionText: What is the reliable range for a resistance meter on timber?
questions.explanation: Resistance meters are reliable on timber from about 6% to 30%. Many meters display much higher numbers, but the display range is not the reliable range.

questions.questionText: A stud reads 45% on the timber scale on day 1. How do you write it?
questions.explanation: Readings above 30% must be treated as qualitative only. A percentage with a decimal, or an accuracy claim, promises precision the meter does not have in that zone.

questions.questionText: When does quantitative tracking of a wet stud start?
questions.explanation: Below 30% a corrected timber reading is a measurement again, so tracking in percent can start. Above 30% you record the reading as qualitative and keep re-reading.

questions.questionText: What does equilibrium moisture content describe?
options: Moisture content timber reaches when fully oven dried
Moisture content above which timber starts shrinking more
Moisture content where the meter reads most accurately
Level where timber neither gains nor loses water
questions.explanation: EMC is the balance point between the timber and the surrounding air, so it changes with the room. It is not the oven-dry state, the shrinkage point or an instrument setting.

questions.questionText: An office is steady at 22 °C, 45 %RH with EMC 8.4%. Unaffected skirting reads 8.6%. What does that suggest?
options: Wet skirting needing immediate stripping out
Good dry baseline close to EMC
Meter fault needing replacement before use
Reading invalid above reliable range limits
questions.explanation: A reading within a fraction of a percent of the room's EMC is what dry timber should read there. It is a trustworthy baseline, not a sign of water or a faulty meter.

questions.questionText: Why do humid tropical rooms give a higher EMC?
options: Warm air always dries timber more quickly
Tropical timber species always contain less water
More humid air holds balanced timber higher
Pin meters read lower in humid rooms
questions.explanation: Timber balances with the air around it, so higher relative humidity at a given temperature means a higher EMC. A reading around 14% in the tropics can be normal.

questions.questionText: Plasterboard shows 64 and unaffected plasterboard 12. Percent or points?
questions.explanation: The meter is not calibrated for plasterboard, so the numbers are points that only compare with the same material unaffected. Wetness alone does not make a reading a percentage.

questions.questionText: Why do qualitative readings carry no decimal places?
options: Decimals are banned by every meter maker
Decimals take longer to enter in reports
Decimals only apply to the points scale
Decimals claim precision the meter lacks there
questions.explanation: A decimal implies the meter can resolve that fine a difference, which it cannot above the reliable range or off its calibrated material. Whole numbers state only what the meter can support.

questions.questionText: What do you compare unaffected timber skirting against?
options: The highest reading on the wet wall
The maximum value the meter scale shows
The room EMC from temperature and humidity
The reading taken at the last visit
questions.explanation: Dry timber reads what the room's temperature and humidity say it should, so the EMC is the check on a baseline. The other options do not describe where dry timber should sit.

questions.questionText: A bearer at 9 °C is colder than the 20 °C calibration. What do you do?
questions.explanation: Cold wood conducts less, so a resistance meter reads it too dry and the correction is added. Subtracting is for warm wood.

questions.questionText: A rafter at 35 °C reads 14.0%, calibrated at 20 °C. What is the corrected reading?
questions.explanation: Wood 15 °C warmer than calibration gives 15 ÷ 5.6 × 0.5 = 1.34, subtracted from 14.0. Adding it would give 15.3% and be wrong because warm wood reads too wet.

questions.questionText: What should you record with a corrected pin reading?
options: Only the final corrected percent figure
The weather forecast for that day
Wood temperature and the correction applied
The occupant's name and the address
questions.explanation: Someone else can only check the correction if the wood temperature and the amount applied are written next to it. A bare corrected figure cannot be traced.

questions.questionText: Where does a species correction come from?
options: The table supplied with your meter
The offsets printed in this lesson
A rule of thumb from experience
The builder's memory of the species
questions.explanation: Species tables are specific to each meter design, so the correction comes from your own meter's documentation. The offsets in this course are invented for practice.

questions.questionText: A radiata stud at 11 °C reads 19.0%. The invented table gives +1, species first. What is the corrected reading?
questions.explanation: Species first gives 20.0%, then 9 °C colder adds 9 ÷ 5.6 × 0.5 = 0.80, giving 20.8%. Stopping at 20.0% skips the temperature step and 19.8% skips the species step.

questions.questionText: What do you do when the species is unknown?
options: Assume radiata pine and report normally
Use the highest species offset available
Skip the reading and keep moving
Say species unknown; treat as estimate
questions.explanation: Do not present a guessed setting as measured. Say the species is unknown and treat the figure as an estimate until you can confirm it.

questions.questionText: Which condition can push a pin reading above the true moisture content?
questions.explanation: Treatment chemicals are electrolytes that raise conductivity, so the meter reads high. Cold wood reads low, and insulated pins or correct alignment reduce error.

questions.questionText: Treated plates read 26% and untreated studs 17% after a storm-tide flood. How do you report them?
options: Report both, note treatment, seawater, track trend
Report 26% only, because it is highest
Report the average of both as 21.5%
Discard the plates and keep the studs
questions.explanation: Both readings go in the record with a note that treatment and seawater may make the plates read high. The trend over several visits is more reliable than either single number.

questions.questionText: Is the conductivity of wood higher along or across the grain?
questions.explanation: Wood conducts best along the grain, in the approximate ratio 1.0 to 0.55 to 0.50 for longitudinal, radial and tangential. That is one reason pin orientation matters.

questions.questionText: In the worked example, which correction comes first?
questions.explanation: The invented maker's table says to apply species first, then temperature. Your own maker's documentation sets the real order, and you write it down.

questions.questionText: Which temperature goes on the worksheet with the reading?
questions.explanation: The correction depends on the temperature of the wood where you read it, so that is the figure to record. Air temperature and thermostat settings can differ widely from the wood.

questions.questionText: Why can seawater lead to a false high reading?
options: Salt makes timber physically absorb more
Electrolytes in the wood raise conductivity
Salt crystals stop the pins touching
Seawater cools the wood below calibration
questions.explanation: Seawater leaves salts that raise the wood's conductivity, so the meter reads high without extra water. Cooler wood would read low, not high.

quizzes.title: CARSI Professional Moisture Meters — Module 4 check

questions.questionText: Why is one stud reading of 14% not enough to approve relining a 4 m wall?
options: Water wicks unevenly, so one stud misleads
Studs never hold water, so skip them
Fourteen percent is above the QBCC limit
A single reading needs no temperature correction
questions.explanation: Water moves unevenly through framing, so one stud can read dry while the plate or another stud is still wet. 14% is also below the 16% QBCC figure, so the problem is coverage, not the number.

questions.questionText: Why do you read the bottom plate as well as the studs?
options: It always reads the same as studs
It lets you skip the control stud
It is often the wettest framing piece
It is the only piece pins reach
questions.explanation: The plate sits at the bottom where water collects, so it is often the last piece to dry. In the worked example the plate corrects to 16.6%, still above 16%.

questions.questionText: Below what moisture content does the QBCC guide say relining can go ahead, with the framing sound?
questions.explanation: The QBCC flood guide gives 16%, and it also says the framing must present as sound. 9% to 13% is the normal in-service range, which is why a lower figure is tempting but not the limit.

questions.questionText: Where does the plasterboard baseline reading come from?
options: The wettest point on the wall
Known-dry plasterboard in an unaffected room
A printed table from the maker
Whatever reading the meter shows first
questions.explanation: The baseline is the same board, same meter and same mode in a dry area, so it shows what dry reads today. A table or the wettest point cannot tell you that.

questions.questionText: The baseline is 13 points. Readings are 24 at 600 mm and 14 at 800 mm. Where is the wet boundary?
questions.explanation: The boundary is where readings return to the baseline. At 800 mm the reading is 14, within one point of 13, while 600 mm is still high at 24.

questions.questionText: Why is the plasterboard baseline re-read at every visit?
options: Conditions shift, so old baselines mislead
Plasterboard changes colour when it dries
The meter loses its calibration daily
The maker’s requirement changes each week
questions.explanation: Drying changes the air in the building, so the dry reference moves. Without a same-day baseline you cannot tell drying from a building-wide change.

questions.questionText: Why can a surface reading not clear a slab for vinyl planks?
options: It measures humidity at the wrong depth
It is qualitative and misses deep moisture
It cannot be used on any concrete
It is only valid after seven days
questions.explanation: A surface meter gives a shallow, qualitative number in points. The QBCC guide names a flooring hygrometer as the most reliable test, and ARFA treats surface results as indicative only.

questions.questionText: The room is 23 °C and 68% RH, the dew point is 16.8 °C and the slab is 16.5 °C. What does that mean?
options: Slab is above dew point, readings reliable
Slab and air are equal, no issue
Slab is below dew point, condensation possible
Dew point is irrelevant for concrete slabs
questions.explanation: A surface colder than the dew point can collect condensation, which pushes surface readings up. Here the slab is 0.3 °C below it, so the surface numbers cannot be trusted alone.

questions.questionText: Who sets the hygrometer test method and acceptance limit for a slab?
options: Floor covering maker and the current standard
Whoever owns the pinless meter on site
The technician’s experience of similar earlier jobs
The surface reading taken on the day
questions.explanation: The acceptance limit comes from the floor covering manufacturer and the named standard, which this course does not restate. A surface reading or personal experience cannot set it.

questions.questionText: Is a waffle pod part of the concrete thickness?
options: Yes, use the full nominal slab thickness
Yes, because foam carries load like concrete
No, set depth from concrete over it
No, pods never affect any test point
questions.explanation: The pod is foam, so only the concrete over it counts. In the example the hole depth must be set from 85 mm of topping, not the 310 mm rib depth.

questions.questionText: A test hole breaks into white foam. What do you record?
options: Slab is dry because foam is dry
Point invalid for concrete RH, choose another
Drill deeper until you reach concrete again
Move the probe up and read anyway
questions.explanation: A probe in foam does not measure the concrete, so the point is invalid. Moving the probe up or drilling deeper to rescue it gives a result that does not mean what it appears to.

questions.questionText: No safe, valid in-situ test point exists. Can a surface reading stand in?
options: Yes, if the reading is low
Yes, once the slab is warm
Yes, provided the installer agrees verbally
No, record no valid in-situ result
questions.explanation: A surface reading is not a basis for accepting a floor, so it cannot replace a valid test. Record “no valid in-situ result” and seek an accepted alternative.

questions.questionText: A pinless scan shows stripes every 450 mm. What does that spacing suggest?
options: Fixings or studs behind the board
A burst pipe behind the board
Salt contamination spread across the wall
A flat battery in the meter
questions.explanation: Regular spacing that matches stud centres points to the frame, not to water, which does not form even stripes. Pins beside a stripe then confirm it.

questions.questionText: One ceiling sheet reads 60 points while the sheets either side read 15, with no stain. What do you check first?
options: Whether the roof is leaking above
Whether the room is too cold
Whether that sheet has foil backing
Whether the battery has gone flat
questions.explanation: A uniform high across exactly one sheet points to the board, such as foil backing or metal behind it. Water rarely stops at the edge of one sheet.

questions.questionText: How do you confirm that a suspected stud-line false high is not moisture?
options: Another pinless scan at the same spot
Pins in the board beside the stripe
Scan again more quickly along the stripe
Ignore it because stripes are always dry
questions.explanation: Pins measure at the tips and do not respond to a stud behind the board, so a baseline reading beside the stripe confirms it. Repeating a pinless scan only repeats the same error.

questions.questionText: What read pattern do you use on a framing wall before relining?
options: One stud at mid height near corner
Only the bottom plate at one end
Several studs at three heights plus plate
Every stud, but at one height only
questions.explanation: Water wicks unevenly, so the wall needs several studs, three heights and the plate to be represented. A single point or a single height can miss the wet part.

questions.questionText: What comes before tracing the boundary on plasterboard?
options: Read a known-dry baseline of same board
Mark the boundary using a pencil first
Convert every reading into percent moisture content
Wait three days before taking any readings
questions.explanation: Without the baseline you do not know what dry reads on that board, so you cannot find where readings return to it. Points are not converted to percent.

questions.questionText: How should surface readings on concrete be treated?
options: Quantitative proof once corrected for temperature
Qualitative pointers, not proof of dryness
Valid only below the dew point
Equal to an in-situ hygrometer result
questions.explanation: Surface readings are shallow and qualitative, so they point to where to test but cannot clear a slab. A hygrometer test decides.

quizzes.title: CARSI Professional Moisture Meters — Module 5 check

questions.questionText: Why is comparing two moisture meters the weakest check?
questions.explanation: Two meters can be wrong in the same direction, so agreement proves little. The maker’s check device or reference block is a fixed reference, which is why it comes first.

questions.questionText: A meter still fails after a new battery and cleaning. What do you do?
questions.explanation: A meter that fails after a battery change and cleaning is out of service until it is repaired and checked. Comparing it with another meter is the weakest check, so it cannot clear it.

questions.questionText: Your pin meter last passed its check on Monday and fails on Wednesday. Which readings do you flag?
questions.explanation: The last good check is the last point you can vouch for the meter, so every reading after it is in question. Flagging them lets you re-read with a checked meter.

questions.questionText: A technician leaves pins in a wet stud, then reads an unaffected stud. Which mistake is this?
questions.explanation: The pins carry moisture and contamination from the wet stud to the next one, which can lift the reading and spread contamination to the control area. Wiping the pins after each reading prevents it.

questions.questionText: A file shows 9% on bearers in a 6 °C subfloor, and the meter was calibrated at 20 °C. How much correction applies?
questions.explanation: The wood is 14 °C colder than the calibration temperature: 14 ÷ 5.6 × 0.5 = 1.25, added because the wood is colder. Subtracting is for wood warmer than the calibration temperature.

questions.questionText: Which habit prevents mistake 3, wrong electrode, mode or scale?
questions.explanation: Mistake 3 is a settings error, so the habit is to set and record the mode, scale and species before the first reading. Spare batteries, wiping pins and the morning check each prevent a different mistake.

questions.questionText: Why is a reading at the dehumidifier outlet unreliable as the room condition?
options: Sensors cannot measure warm moving air
It shows outlet air, not room
The sensor needs a weekly check
questions.explanation: Air at the outlet describes what the machine is putting out, not the air the timber sits in. The room reading, taken clear of the outlet, is the one to compare with the material.

questions.questionText: Two rooms both read 50% RH, at 18 °C and 26 °C. Which holds more water vapour?
options: Both rooms hold exactly the same
Neither can be compared at all
questions.explanation: Warm air holds more water at the same RH: about 10.5 g/kg at 26 °C against about 6.4 g/kg at 18 °C. That is why you compare rooms in g/kg, not RH alone.

questions.questionText: Why let a hygrometer settle in the room before you read it?
questions.explanation: A sensor carried in from another place needs time to reach the room’s air, so an early reading describes where it has been. Follow the maker’s settling time before you log the number.

questions.questionText: What does tagging a meter out mean?
options: Downgraded to scanning dry areas only
Kept as back-up for concrete slabs
Given a new calibration serial tag
Marked out of service until checked
questions.explanation: Tag-out labels the instrument out of service until it is repaired and checked, so nobody picks it up by mistake. It is not a downgrade or a back-up role.

questions.questionText: What is the maker’s reference block used for?
questions.explanation: The reference block or plate is the fixed reference for a pinless meter. A pin meter uses the maker’s check device instead, which is the tempting mix-up.

questions.questionText: What is the correct order of the morning checks?
questions.explanation: The routine starts with the meter’s own self-check, then the two moisture meter checks, then the hygrometer pair, and ends by writing the result in the log. The log comes last because it records the outcome.

quizzes.title: CARSI Professional Moisture Meters — Module 6 check

questions.questionText: Where does the dry standard for hallway framing come from?
options: A chart of average timber moisture figures
The wettest stud found at first scan
An unaffected stud in the same building
A figure quoted by the building owner
questions.explanation: The dry standard is the same material, unaffected, in the same building, read with the same meter, mode and scale on the same visit. A published average cannot account for this building, this season or this meter.

questions.questionText: The control reads 11.7% and QBCC gives below 16%. Which framing goal does the lesson use?
options: 16% exactly, because the guide says so
Whatever the meter reads when fans stop
Exactly 11.7%, the same as the control
questions.explanation: The goal is no wetter than the 16% relining figure and close to the dry standard, so the worked example sets 14% or less. It is written on day 1, not read off the meter at the end.

questions.questionText: The control stud reads 11.7% but the room EMC is 18.6%. What do you do first?
options: Trust the stud; disregard atmospheric readings
Average the two figures and record
Raise the goal until it matches
Re-check the air, control and settings
questions.explanation: A gap that large means one of the inputs is wrong: the air reading, the control location, the species setting or the temperature correction. Averaging or moving the goal hides the fault instead of finding it.

questions.questionText: Why does the map use fixed, numbered reading points?
options: It lets technicians read anywhere they like
Each visit compares the same spot again
It removes the need for any control
It makes corrections unnecessary on later days
questions.explanation: A trend means something only if each day reads the same point with the same settings. Fixed points do not replace the control, and corrections still apply on every visit.

questions.questionText: On day 5 the control reads 11.6% and P1 has fallen to 16.3%. What does this show?
options: The meter has drifted and needs replacement
P1 has already reached its 14% goal
The control stud is wet and unreliable
Drying is working; the building is steady
questions.explanation: The control has stayed near 11.7% all week, so nothing has changed for the whole building and the fall at P1 is drying. P1 at 16.3% is still above the 14% goal.

questions.questionText: P1 reads 24.2%, 19.8% and 16.3% on days 1, 3 and 5. What is the trend?
options: Falling, but still above its goal
Rising slowly and above its goal
Flat, with drying clearly stalled here
Falling, and already below its goal
questions.explanation: Each visit is lower than the last, so the point is drying, but 16.3% is still above the 14% goal. Comparing with the goal, not only with yesterday, is what the map is for.

questions.questionText: Day 7 framing readings (corrected) are 15.8%, 15.1%, 14.6% and 15.5%, and the framing is sound. What does the QBCC condition say?
options: Relining must wait until all readings reach 14%
Relining must wait until the slab is tested
Relining may go ahead; all are below 16%
Relining must wait until framing reads under 12%
questions.explanation: QBCC asks for framing below 16% that presents as sound, and every reading is below 16%. The 14% figure is your own goal, which you record separately as not yet met.

questions.questionText: Boards at 13.5% go into a room with an EMC of 12.0%. What does the Queensland timbers guidance indicate?
options: Acclimatisation is required; the difference is 1.5%
Acclimatisation is not indicated; difference is 1.5%
Acclimatisation is not indicated; difference exceeds 2%
Acclimatisation is required; the difference exceeds 2%
questions.explanation: The difference is 13.5 − 12.0 = 1.5%, inside the 2% figure, so acclimatisation is not indicated. It would be considered only if the difference were more than 2%.

questions.questionText: Who decides acclimatisation and floor-covering acceptance limits?
options: The installer and the product manufacturer
The drying technician, using the meter
The loss adjuster, working from photographs
The occupants, judging by touch alone
questions.explanation: You supply readings, the dry standard, the goal and a conclusion in writing; the installer and manufacturer answer for the floor-covering and acclimatisation decisions. A meter reading cannot set a product limit.

questions.questionText: Outside air is 15.56 g/kg and the hallway 11.96 g/kg. What follows?
options: Ventilating would dry the hallway much faster
Outside air is drier, so open windows
Humidity ratio cannot compare indoor with outdoors
Ventilating would add water to the hallway
questions.explanation: Outside air holds more water per kilogram than the hallway, so bringing it in would add water. Humidity ratio in g/kg is exactly the number that lets you compare the two.

questions.questionText: Which reading acts as the control for the air in the case?
options: The laundry floor at its wettest point
questions.explanation: The lounge is the unaffected room, so it shows what the building normally holds. The hallway is the drying space and outside is the third reading, not the control.

questions.questionText: What must the written day 1 statement contain beyond the readings?
options: A guarantee that everything is dry
Only photographs, without any meter settings
Settings, standard, goal and the rule
The adjuster’s name and claim number
questions.explanation: A defensible statement carries the settings, the dry standard, the goal and the rule you applied. It never promises that the job is dry before the readings say so.

questions.questionText: Which checklist line comes straight after the morning calibration check?
options: Air readings for space, control and outside
The final written drying-status statement for sign-off
Reading the fixed map points each visit
Setting the drying goal for the relining
questions.explanation: The checklist runs safety, the calibration check, then the air readings, because the air decides what the timber should read and whether ventilating helps. The statement comes last.

questions.questionText: How is a laundry plasterboard reading of 61 recorded?
options: As 61% moisture content in the board
As 61% once corrected for wood temperature
As 61 times the unaffected board reading
As 61 points on the reference scale
questions.explanation: Plasterboard is read in points on the reference scale, against unaffected board, never as a percentage. A figure above 30 is qualitative whatever the material.

questions.questionText: What must a written drying-status statement contain?
options: Approximate readings, rounded to whole numbers
Readings, settings, standard, goal and rule
The drying goal, without any readings
Instrument settings, without the dry standard
questions.explanation: Anyone who was not on site needs the readings, the settings, the dry standard, the goal and the rule you applied to check the conclusion. Leaving any one out makes the statement impossible to repeat.

quizzes.lessonTitle: Final knowledge check: mixed practice across all modules
quizzes.title: CARSI Professional Moisture Meters — Final Knowledge Check

questions.questionText: A sample weighs 412.6 g wet and 356.0 g oven-dry. What is its moisture content?
questions.explanation: (412.6 − 356.0) ÷ 356.0 × 100 = 15.9%. The divisor is the oven-dry mass.

questions.questionText: What do uninsulated pins on a resistance meter report?
options: The wettest layer that they touch
The average of the whole piece
Only the wood at the tips
Only the moisture in the coating
questions.explanation: Uninsulated pins sense the lowest resistance along their length, so they report the wettest layer they touch (Wood Handbook ch. 13).

questions.questionText: Which part of the material dominates a pinless (dielectric) reading?
questions.explanation: The field weakens rapidly with depth, so the surface layers dominate (Wood Handbook ch. 13).

questions.questionText: To read the average moisture of a 45 mm stud that is wetter inside, set insulated pins to about:
questions.explanation: One-fifth to one-quarter of 45 mm is 9 to 11.25 mm (Wood Handbook ch. 13).

questions.questionText: How should a plasterboard reading of 64 on a reference scale be reported?
questions.explanation: Reference-scale readings are qualitative: report points against the same material unaffected.

questions.questionText: Above what timber reading does the Wood Handbook treat meter readings as qualitative only?
questions.explanation: Readings greater than 30% must be considered only qualitative (Wood Handbook ch. 13).

questions.questionText: What in-service moisture content range does the QBCC flood guide give for timber in houses?
questions.explanation: QBCC says timber in houses normally has an in-service moisture content of between 9% and 13%.

questions.questionText: A stud at 9 °C reads 18.0% on a resistance meter calibrated at 20 °C. What is the corrected reading?
questions.explanation: 11 °C colder: 11 ÷ 5.6 × 0.5 = 0.98, added because the wood is cold: 19.0%.

questions.questionText: A rafter at 35 °C reads 14.0% on a meter calibrated at 20 °C. Which way does the correction go?
questions.explanation: Warm wood reads high on a resistance meter, so subtract: 15 ÷ 5.6 × 0.5 = 1.34; 12.7%.

questions.questionText: Where should a species correction for your meter come from?
questions.explanation: Species tables are specific to each meter design; use the one supplied with your instrument.

questions.questionText: Which of these can raise a pin reading above the true moisture content?
questions.explanation: Salts and treatments raise conductivity (Wood Handbook ch. 4). Cold wood reads low, not high.

questions.questionText: Framing must be below which moisture content before relining, under the QBCC guide?
questions.explanation: Relining should wait until timber wall framing is below 16% and the framing is sound (QBCC).

questions.questionText: What does the QBCC guide call the most reliable test for dryness of a concrete floor?
questions.explanation: “For concrete floors, the most reliable test for dryness is a flooring hygrometer.” (QBCC, p. 5)

questions.questionText: A pinless scan shows vertical stripes of high readings every 450 mm on a dry wall. Most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Regular spacing matching stud centres points to fixings or studs; confirm with pins beside a stripe.

questions.questionText: Which daily calibration check is the weakest on its own?
questions.explanation: Two meters can be wrong in the same direction, so a meter-to-meter comparison is only a back-up.

questions.questionText: Which of these is one of the six common meter mistakes?
questions.explanation: Pins left in wet material carry moisture and contamination to the next reading.

questions.questionText: What is the dry standard for a wet plasterboard wall?
options: Same board unaffected, read same way
The meter maker’s published dry value
The highest reading on day one
questions.explanation: The dry standard is the same material, unaffected, in the same building, read the same way on the same visit.

questions.questionText: The hallway is 23 °C and 68% RH. Which EMC should dry timber there approach?
questions.explanation: Wood Handbook eq. 4-5 gives 12.5% for 23 °C, 68% RH.

questions.questionText: A laundry slab is at 16.5 °C and the room dew point is 16.8 °C. What does that mean for surface readings?
options: They prove the slab is dry
They may include some surface condensation
They prove moisture deep in slab
They need a species correction applied
questions.explanation: A surface below the dew point can collect condensation, so surface readings cannot separate it from slab moisture.

questions.questionText: Boards arrive at 13.5% for a room whose EMC is 12.0%. Under the CTIQ guidance, is acclimatisation indicated?
questions.explanation: The difference is 1.5%, inside the 2% figure in Construction timbers in Queensland; the installer still decides.
